newsitem.title: USA: Fla. charges Puerto Rico with dumping felons.
newsitem.headline: Fla. charges Puerto Rico with dumping felons.

text.p: The confrontation last June 15 seemed like just another in Florida's wearying litany of violent acts -- police in a standoff with a group of armed men.
But this time Florida Highway Patrol officers had run into an armed group of agents from the Puerto Rico Department of Justice.

And though it seemed that gunfire might be exchanged while the two sides doubted one another's identities, the Puerto Rican officers were able to establish that they were agents on legitimate business, relocating a participant in the U.S. territory's witness protection programme.

The incident led to widespread speculation that Puerto Rico was dumping violent criminals and drug dealers in Florida, particularly in Orlando, scene of the June confrontation, a central Florida city with a large Puerto Rican population.
And it prompted Florida Gov. Lawton Chiles to ask for a formal agreement between the state and the U.S. territory to make sure Florida received information about all relocations.
The Orlando Sentinel has published a series of articles this autumn describing the shipment of drug dealers and other criminals from Puerto Rico to Florida.

On October 11 two Central Florida sheriffs, concerned about the reports that drug dealers had been dumped in their state, called on the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the U.S. Justice Department to investigate Puerto Rico's actions.

"We're working day and night to arrest drug dealers," Osceola County Sheriff Charlie Croft told a news conference. "Now we find out that they have been shipping dozens of new drug dealers into Orange and Osceola Counties. This is a drug dealer's dream come true: Deal heroin and win an all-expenses paid vacation to Florida."
A U.S. congressional fact-finding hearing was held in Orlando this week over the allegations.
On Saturday state officials said the two sides were close to reaching some kind of a formal accord on the issue.
"We've said all along that we believe we can work this out with the government of Puerto Rico," said Chiles spokeswoman Karen Pankowski. "We're confident that we'll reach an agreement."

Chiles did not participate in the congressional hearing, which was held on Thursday, but on October 28 he sent Puerto Rico Gov. Pedro Rossello a memorandum of understanding asking the territory to provide Florida with information including fingerprints and in some cases DNA samples, when witnesses are sent to the state.

Some 329 people have been relocated to the U.S. mainland, including 95 to Florida, since the Caribbean U.S. territory began its witness relocation programme 10 years ago. During that time, Puerto Rican officials have not informed federal or local officials of the transfers.
Miguel Gierbolini, deputy director of the Puerto Rico Justice Department's Special Investigations Bureau, disputed allegations that Puerto Rico was shipping many criminals to Florida.

For example he said during the hearing that only six of the 40 programme participants sent to the Orlando area had a prior criminal history and that none of the 40 had been convicted of any criminal act since arriving.
Gierbolini said he had not done enough research to say exactly what proportion of all the programme participants had criminal records, but said the overall ratio was similar to those in Orlando.

State witness protection programmes are not uncommon. Nine U.S. states, including Florida, have programmes in place. And there is no federal oversight of the programmes, a fact that worries Florida Department of Law Enforcement Assistant Commissioner Robert Cumming, who testified before the committee.

"When a witness with a past criminal history is relocated into a new community, there is always a risk that the person will revert to crime," Cumming said. "The temptation to do so may be greater if the person is placed in a new community with the advantage of anonymity."
